title: This Indonesian Volcano Can Kill, But After Dark It Becomes Something Breathtakingly Beautiful
text: As night starts to settle over East Java, Indonesia, the world's colors become more muted. Except, that is, in one place, where one of the most spectacular shows on Earth is about to begin. This is Kawah Ijen, a living volcano in eastern Java. It looks just like any other active volcano. In other words: nothing grows on it, and nothing goes near it if it can be avoided. And yet there are people who regularly have to venture onto the volcano, whatever danger it may pose. The reason is the hot vents on the volcano's slope, which pump out sulfur – something that can be extracted and sold and which, as a result, can help locals earn a living. So at times a number of sulfur miners can be seen hanging around the vents at Kawah Ijen. Some of them press damp rags to their mouths as a barrier against breathing in the toxic sulfur gas. It's an essential precaution for anyone hoping to harvest this bright yellow element. The process, however, has been made easier by ceramic pipes that were attached to one of the volcano's vents. When the sulfur gas rises through the Earth's crust, it enters the pipes, cools into a liquid and eventually turns solid. That's when the workmen break up the sulfur and heave the resulting chunks onto their backs to carry it away. Even so, the miners don't earn much for their labor. In fact, each pound of hard-won sulfur brings them less than 25 cents. Still, the backbreaking work does have some perks – especially for those who toil after the sun has set. Because when night finally falls, an amazing transformation takes place.

title: Shopify Wiped Our Store Off The Internet While I Was Fulfilling 55 Orders
text: To launch a Return Of Kings t-shirt shop, I chose Shopify because it is so much easier to launch than a self-hosted store. I signed up, paid for one year of service, and ran a pre-launch with a small group of readers, which produced 55 orders. While I was fulfilling them, Shopify pulled the plug on the whole store without warning, both the public storefront and the administrative backend holding all our data. Because of Shopify's decision, my customers couldn't check their order status, I had no way of telling them what had happened, and I couldn't fulfill the remaining orders. They left both me and 55 individuals in the lurch for no legitimate reason, forcing me to threaten legal action just to get enough information to finish fulfilling all the orders. There are many open source options for hosting a web store. The trouble with them is that creating and maintaining the store takes extra time compared to services like Shopify, Squarespace, Bigcommerce, Magento, and others. To get the ROK store running as fast as possible, I went with Shopify because of their competitive prices, not realizing I would pay a far greater price down the road. Once the store was set up, featuring photos of yours truly in our first t-shirt, I gathered email addresses from those most interested in taking part in the pre-launch. I emailed this group to announce the store, and 55 of them took action, ordering a t-shirt or two.

title: UK PM May to give Brexit speech in Italy on Sept. 22, spokesman says
text: Prime Minister Theresa May will deliver a speech on Britain's future relationship with the European Union on Sept. 22 in the Italian city of Florence, her spokesman said on Wednesday. The speech will concentrate on the kind of ties Britain wants with the EU after it leaves the bloc in March 2019, a subject British negotiators have been eager to discuss with a so-far reluctant Brussels. “The prime minister wanted to give a speech on the UK’s future relationship with Europe in its historical heart,” May's spokesman told reporters. She will stress the government's desire for a deep and special partnership with the European Union once the UK leaves the EU. Negotiations on the terms of the divorce have made limited progress since May triggered a two-year countdown to Brexit. That has led the EU to warn that talks on the future relationship between the two could be delayed beyond their planned October start. The September round of Brexit talks has been put back by a week to the end of the month, in what EU diplomats said was a move intended to let May give her speech. Britain said the rescheduling was meant to give both sides more time to make progress. May's speech could lend weight to the British push to move the talks forward, which ministers say is crucial to providing certainty for businesses worried about how Brexit will affect their ability to trade across borders. Her choice of venue, a city celebrated as the birthplace of the Renaissance and made rich by international trade and banking, is a nod to the kind of free-trading relationship Britain wants to keep with Europe and develop around the world.

title: The Worst Outcome for Republicans: A Trump Victory
text: Republicans head into the fall campaign in moods that run from grim foreboding to howling despair. They worry that Donald Trump will not merely lose but lose so badly that he drags hordes of other candidates down with him, costing the GOP control of the U.S. Senate and possibly the House. This election could be the party's worst debacle since 1964. Yet Republicans do not appear to have prepared for an even greater catastrophe that could happen Nov. 8: Trump winning. In that case, they would not be stuck with him for just the next two months. They would be stuck with him for his entire presidency, and they would have to answer for him forever. title: Ex-House speaker Hastert’s sentencing pushed back to April
text: A federal judge on Thursday delayed until April the sentencing of Dennis Hastert, who was convicted last year of a financial crime, because the former U.S. House speaker was still recovering from a stroke and a life-threatening infection. Hastert pleaded guilty in October to a federal charge of “structuring”, evading bank reporting rules by withdrawing large sums of cash in smaller amounts, in a hush-money case that grew out of allegations of sexual misconduct. The 74-year-old, once among the most powerful politicians in the country, was hospitalized in early November after a fall, his attorney, John Gallo, told U.S. District Judge Thomas Durkin. Gallo said Hastert was treated for a spinal infection that required surgery and for a severe blood infection, and suffered a stroke, nearly dying. Durkin moved Hastert's sentencing to April 8 from Feb. 29. Hastert currently needs 24-hour care. He can feed himself and is articulate, but a doctor has said he should not leave his home except to go to the hospital. Gallo said Hastert is still able to help prepare for his sentencing, and his doctors would have a better sense of his prognosis in a month. Hastert faces up to five years in prison, but prosecutors have recommended a sentence of six months or less in exchange for his guilty plea. Hastert admitted paying $1.7 million in cash to a person he had known for decades to buy that person's silence and compensate for past misconduct toward that person. Prosecutors did not specify the misconduct, but unnamed law enforcement officials have told media that it was sexual and involved someone Hastert knew when he was a high school teacher and coach in his hometown of Yorkville, Illinois, in the 1960s and 1970s.

title: THAILAND THREATENS TO PROSECUTE FACEBOOK Over Humiliating Video Of King Strolling Through Mall In Yellow Crop Top, Covered In Tattoos
text: Embarrassing footage of Thailand's king in a crop top showing off his tattoos has led authorities to threaten action against Facebook. The video of King Maha Vajiralongkorn strolling through a shopping centre with a woman was widely shared on the social network. But Thai authorities have threatened to press charges if it is still up at 10am tomorrow. The video shows the monarch, who took the throne last year after the death of his father, with a number of tattoos on his arms, stomach, and back. Under Thailand's strict lese-majeste laws, people can be jailed for up to 15 years for sharing material that insults the monarchy. The social network has geo-blocked the video, but Thai authorities say 131 pages containing the illicit video are still available. Takorn Tantasith, secretary-general of the National Broadcasting and Telecommunications Commission, said: “If even a single illicit page remains, we will immediately discuss what legal steps to take against Facebook Thailand.” Last week the Thai Internet Service Provider Association emailed Facebook chief executive Mark Zuckerberg demanding that the posts be blocked, the Bangkok Post reports.
